title: The Default Effect

scenes.vo: In Austria, almost everyone is a registered organ donor. In neighbouring Germany, only about 12 percent. Why?
These are similar countries, with similar cultures and similar values.

scenes.text: Germany: tick a box to *opt in*
scenes.vo: The difference is a single checkbox. In Germany, you tick a box to opt in.

scenes.text: Austria: tick a box to *opt out*
scenes.vo: In Austria, you're a donor by default. You tick a box to opt out.

scenes.text:
Most people just…
*don't tick the box*
scenes.vo: And most people simply never tick the box. Whatever the default is, wins.
This is the default effect. Defaults feel like a recommendation, and changing them takes effort.
Apps know this well. Auto-renew, pre-ticked add-ons, notifications switched on.

scenes.text: Audit your defaults. Make good habits the *default*.
scenes.vo: So audit your defaults. Set up the auto-save, turn off the auto-renew, and make good habits the default.

scenes.text:
Follow *@inquisitive_bytes*
for a daily byte of behaviour science
scenes.vo: Follow Inquisitive Bytes for a daily byte of behaviour science.

caption:
One checkbox, and the donor rate goes from 12% to 99%. ☑️ Defaults are among the most powerful forces in behaviour science.

Which default are you changing today? 👇
source: Johnson, E. J. & Goldstein, D. (2003). Do Defaults Save Lives? Science, 302(5649).
